title: Dual Goal Representations
one_liner: Instead of encoding goals as raw states, encode them as the time-distance to reach every other state in the world.
lead: When a robot learns to reach goals, it usually remembers goals as pixel images or position vectors. But those representations are fragile—they break when the robot moves to a new room or the camera angle changes. This paper proposes a radically different idea: encode a goal not as what it looks like, but as how long it takes to reach from every other place in the environment. This time-distance signature stays the same no matter what the goal looks like or how the robot's sensors change, and it contains exactly the information the robot needs to plan.

paras: In goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, an agent learns to reach any target state from any starting point. The usual approach: train a policy that takes two inputs—the current state and the goal state—and outputs an action. But the goal is encoded using the same representation as the current state (pixels, joint angles, etc.). This creates a fragility: if you move the robot to a new room, or the lighting changes, that goal representation stops being useful. A goal that was a sharp image of the red cup is now a blurry image of the red cup, and the policy gets confused.

A beginner might try to make the goal representation more abstract—say, by learning a latent embedding through a neural network. But if the agent only sees offline data (collected trajectories with no new interactions), the embedding will still overfit to the specifics of that data. When you swap in a new robot or environment, the embedding collapses.

callout.html: A goal's meaning is not what it looks like; it is how long it takes to reach from everywhere else.

paras: The paper changes how goals are represented. Instead of encoding a goal as its raw appearance or position, it encodes a goal as a learned vector (a list of numbers) that was trained to capture the time-distance from every state to that goal.

hidden.name: Temporal distance to goal
paras: This is a single number: starting from state s, how many steps on average does it take to reach goal g in the optimal policy? It is an invisible quantity—you never directly see it—but it reveals the true structure of the environment's dynamics. Unlike the goal's appearance, this number is invariant (stays the same) no matter what robot body you use or what the lighting is.

The paper estimates this quantity by training a value function—a neural network that learns to predict the temporal distance from any state-goal pair. The value function takes two inputs (current state and goal), and outputs a number representing steps-to-goal. Once trained, the goal part of the network (called the goal embedding) becomes the dual goal representation.

heat.caption: Darker means longer time to reach the goal from that state. Time-distances anchor the goal's meaning.

reads.html: Each goal has an invisible signature: from your current spot, you are 3 steps away; from over there, you are 7 steps away. That signature is what the policy remembers about the goal.

The temporal distance function d(s, g) is the discounted cumulative cost in the optimal policy. The dual representation φ(g) encodes this entire function by learning it via a value-based offline RL algorithm (IQL), then extracting the goal embedding (the part of the learned network that depends on the goal).

mechanism.h2: Why this works: structure through contrast
paras: The key is that temporal distance depends only on the environment's dynamics (the rules of how the world moves), not on the appearance of states. The same goal in two different rooms has the same time-distances (because the robot takes the same number of steps). So when you train a value function on offline data, it learns to extract this intrinsic structure.

More deeply: a value function V(s, g) predicts steps-to-goal. To make that prediction, it must decompose the input into two parts: something about the current state s (where am I?) and something about the goal g (how far away is it from typical starting points?). The goal part—the embedding φ(g)—becomes a learned signature that captures which states are reachable in how many steps. This signature survives changes to appearance because it throws away visual details and only keeps the relational structure. When noise corrupts an observation (wrong pixel, shifted sensor reading), the time-distances remain the same, so the policy still knows how to act.

math.words: The value function is trained to minimize the gap between predicted steps and actual steps in the offline data, using an expectile loss (a loss function that is more flexible about overfitting to outliers than squared error).
symbols: The actual time-to-goal from state s to goal g, observed in the offline data
What the network's value function predicts
A loss function that penalizes error smoothly, avoiding overconfidence on outliers
The extracted goal embedding, the dual goal representation

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose in the offline data, from state A it took 5 steps to reach goal G.
The value function predicts: V_predicted(A, G) = 4 steps.
Error = 5 - 4 = 1 step. Expectile loss: roughly 1.0 (the penalty grows with error magnitude).
The network updates its internal goal embedding φ(G) to make the prediction closer to 5.
Later, from a different state B, the data shows 3 steps to G. The embedding φ(G) must now predict correctly from B as well.
The embedding learns a shared signature that works across all starting states.

math.note: The goal embedding φ(g) is the part of the value function that depends on the goal; once training is done, this embedding becomes the dual goal representation used by the downstream policy.

charts.title: Naive goal representation (raw state pixels)
charts.note: Raw goal representations collapse when the environment changes.

charts.title: Dual goal representation (time-distance signature)
charts.note: Dual representations stay effective because they encode intrinsic structure (how long it takes), not appearance (what it looks like).

items.html: If the offline data only covers a narrow part of the state space, the value function only learns accurate time-distances in that region. For unseen states, its predictions (and the goal embedding) will be unreliable. Remedy: collect offline data that explores the full environment.

If the value function is undertrained or converges to a bad solution, the goal embedding will encode misleading time-distances. The downstream policy will then make poor decisions. Remedy: ensure the value function training converges before extracting the goal embedding.

If the new environment has fundamentally different dynamics (e.g., the robot becomes much faster, or moves in a different topology), the time-distances from the old environment no longer apply because those distances were learned from the old world's rules. The dual representation survives appearance changes but not changes to how the world actually moves, because time-distances are tied to the world's dynamics, not to visual appearance. Remedy: restrict use to environments with similar dynamics.
Train the value function on diverse offline data that covers many states and goals, verify it converges, then use the goal embedding for downstream policy learning in the same environment class.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple 2D gridworld (a 10x10 grid where the agent moves one square per step). Collect offline data: random trajectories showing the agent reaching 5 different goals. Train a value function on this data to predict time-to-goal. Extract the goal embedding for one goal. Then: (1) use the dual representation in a new downstream policy trained in the same gridworld, (2) add visual noise to the goal observation (blur or shift the pixels), and (3) move to a rotated or reflected version of the same gridworld. The demo should show the policy succeeds in all three cases (original, noisy, rotated), while a naive pixel-based goal representation fails in cases 2 and 3.
demo.closing: The dual representation should maintain >80% success across all three tests (original, noisy, rotated), while naive representations collapse to <40%.
